title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text: Final project for MATH 3262 Mathematical Modeling (Kennesaw State University), December 2023. The report is the main write-up; this page summarizes it.

title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text:
Question
If major hub airports went offline, how would passenger volume redistribute across the rest of the U.S. air network?

title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text:
The Report


Download the report (PDF) Code on GitHub

title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text:
Data
The data is the 2022 T-100 Domestic Segment (All Carriers) file from the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics, which records passenger volumes by month, carrier and route. International routes, airports in Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the U.S. Pacific territories, and airports with less than 0.01% of total passenger volume were dropped. That leaves 236 airports and 12,833 routes, joined to an airport table for locations.

title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text:
Method
Total 2022 passengers on each route are arranged in a matrix V, with origin airports as rows and destination airports as columns. Dividing each row by its sum gives the transition matrix P:
P_{ij} = \frac{V_{ij}}{\sum_k V_{ik}}
Every row of P sums to 1, so P describes a discrete-time Markov chain in which a passenger at airport i moves to airport j with probability proportional to outbound traffic on that route. The stationary distribution \vec{\pi} is the eigenvector of P^T for eigenvalue 1, scaled to sum to 1:
P^T \vec{\pi} = \vec{\pi}, \qquad \textstyle\sum_i \pi_i = 1
It gives each airport’s long-run share of arriving traffic. Multiplying it by total 2022 arriving passengers gives a predicted arriving volume for each airport.
To simulate a disruption, the row and column of each closed airport are removed from V, the rows are re-normalized, and the stationary distribution is recomputed. In both scenarios every remaining airport still has outbound routes, so the re-normalized matrix is a valid transition matrix with a single stationary distribution.

title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text:
Limitations

What-if estimates, not forecasts. Removing a hub and re-normalizing rows assumes passengers redistribute in proportion to existing route volumes, with no airport capacity limits and no new routes.
Memoryless model. A Markov chain assumes the next airport depends only on the current one, which simplifies how real travel works.
One year, domestic only. The data covers domestic 2022 segments, so it leaves out international traffic and year-to-year trends.
External factors. Weather, economic conditions and health crises are not modeled.
Data quality. Errors or gaps in the T-100 data would carry through to the results.

title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text:
Future Work
Extending the model to international routes and external factors, and running Monte Carlo simulations that remove routes at random to study how volumes change statistically. Early Monte Carlo code is in the repository, but it is unfinished and is not part of the report.

title: Modeling Airport Disruptions with a Markov Chain
text:
Tools and Data Sources
R and Quarto, using tidyverse, sf, knitr and kableExtra.
Data: U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics, T-100 Domestic Segment (All Carriers), 2022. Airport lookup tables derived from OpenFlights (Open Database License).

title: Career vs. Volunteer Fire Department Response Times
text: Final project for STAT 3120 (Kennesaw State University), done with Gabriel Salisbury in May 2023. The slide deck is the main write-up; this page summarizes it.

title: Career vs. Volunteer Fire Department Response Times
text:
Question
Is there a statistically significant difference in mean response time (dispatch to arrival) between career and volunteer fire departments? And how does population density relate to response time?

title: Career vs. Volunteer Fire Department Response Times
text:
The Presentation


Download the slides (PDF) Code and data on GitHub

title: Career vs. Volunteer Fire Department Response Times
text:
Data and Cleaning
The data is the public 2019 NFIRS (National Fire Incident Reporting System) incident data, rolled up to one row per department: 11,884 departments, each with at least 30 incidents. Incident-level cleaning, documented on the last slide of the deck, kept geocoded incidents and dropped mutual-aid incidents, incidents with a missing response time, and extreme response times. Departments and census tracts with very few incidents were also dropped.

title: Career vs. Volunteer Fire Department Response Times
text:
Results






ImportantKey Finding



Career departments responded 2.23 minutes faster on average than volunteer departments (5.94 vs. 8.17 minutes, dispatch to arrival, across 11,884 departments). Response times were also faster in denser areas (r = −0.31).

The difference in means is 2.23 minutes (95% CI ±0.075 min). A Welch t-test, used because the variances were unequal, gave t = 57.93, df = 9066.2, p < .0001.


Denser Areas Had Faster Response Times
Across all departments the correlation between population density and mean response time is r = −0.31. Within groups it is r = −0.22 for career departments and r = −0.27 for volunteer departments (all p < .0001). Volunteer departments are concentrated at low density and account for the longest times.



Mean response time against population density, by department type (2019).




Department Type and “Fast” vs. “Slow”
Using the four-level department type against fast/slow, a chi-square test of independence gave χ² = 2310.4, df = 3, p < .0001. Career departments were fast far more often than expected under independence, and volunteer departments were slow far more often.

title: Career vs. Volunteer Fire Department Response Times
text:
Limitations

The unit of analysis is a department’s mean response time, which hides variation between incidents within a department.
With about 12,000 departments, p-values are tiny almost by default. The size of the difference (2.2 minutes) and of the correlations matters more than the significance.
This is observational data. Career and volunteer departments differ in many ways besides staffing model (density, call volume, geography), so the comparison does not show that staffing model causes the difference.
NFIRS is reported by the departments themselves, and reporting quality varies.

title: Predicting House Prices: Linear Regression vs. Tree Models
text: Final project for STAT 3130 (Kennesaw State University), July 2024. The report is the main write-up; this page summarizes it.

title: Predicting House Prices: Linear Regression vs. Tree Models
text:
Question
How do linear regression models with increasing amounts of feature engineering compare with XGBoost and random forest models, run at default settings, at predicting home sale prices? The project also tests whether sale price differs by pool quality.

title: Predicting House Prices: Linear Regression vs. Tree Models
text:
The Report


Download the report (PDF) Code on GitHub

title: Predicting House Prices: Linear Regression vs. Tree Models
text:
Data
The data is the Ames, Iowa housing data from Kaggle’s training set: 1,460 house sales with 79 explanatory variables describing the lot, the building, its condition and the sale. Sale prices are right-skewed, with a median of $163,000 and a mean of $180,921.
The data is split 80/20 with a fixed seed into 1,168 training houses and 292 test houses, and every model uses the same split. Before modeling, the ID column is removed, missing lot frontage is imputed by linear regression on lot area, lot shape and lot configuration, variables with only one value are removed, and categorical variables are converted to dummy variables.

title: Predicting House Prices: Linear Regression vs. Tree Models
text:
Models

Linear regression 1: all variables (259 coefficients after dummy coding).
Linear regression 2: the 47 of 79 predictors that were not significant at the 0.05 level are removed.
Linear regression 3: starting from model 2, 55 training houses with standardized residuals beyond ±2 are removed as outliers, along with two collinear variables and four variables that were no longer significant.
XGBoost and random forest (ranger), both at their default settings with no tuning.

title: Predicting House Prices: Linear Regression vs. Tree Models
text:
Results






ImportantKey Finding



Random forest, with no tuning, predicted test-set prices best (R² 0.919, RMSE $21,117). The best linear model reached only R² 0.444 on the same houses: the linear models overfit the training data and missed badly on a handful of test houses.

Random forest predicts best on every test metric, followed by XGBoost, even with no tuning.
The linear models overfit. They fit the training data well (R² 0.91 to 0.94) but explain much less of the variation in the test houses (R² 0.40 to 0.44). Model 1 estimates 259 coefficients from 1,168 houses.
Model 2 is the best linear model on the test set (R² 0.444). Removing outliers in model 3 improved the training fit but not the test fit. Model 3’s training figures also exclude the 55 houses it removed, so they are not directly comparable with the other two.
A few large errors drive the linear models’ low test R². Their test RMSE is more than three times their MAE. Their typical error (MAE of $20,000 to $22,000) is not far from the tree models’ ($15,000 to $17,000), but on a handful of houses they miss by a very large amount.

Linear regression is easier to interpret and to put into production, while the tree models predict better with far less feature engineering. Which to use depends on whether accuracy or interpretability matters more.

text:

Pool quality was significant in the linear models, so the project tests whether sale price differs by pool quality. Only 7 of the 1,460 houses have a pool:

A one-way ANOVA gave F(3, 1456) = 10.51, p < 0.0001, but the group standard deviations differ too much for its equal-variance assumption to hold. A Kruskal-Wallis test, which does not need that assumption, found no significant difference (χ²(3) = 6.00, p = 0.112). With only seven pools, neither test can say much about pool quality.

title: Predicting House Prices: Linear Regression vs. Tree Models
text:
Limitations

One train/test split. The test metrics come from 292 houses and one random split, with no cross-validation, so they would shift somewhat with a different split.
No tuning. XGBoost and random forest were run at default settings; tuning would likely improve them further.
Skewed prices. Sale prices were modeled in raw dollars even though they are right-skewed, so large errors on expensive houses dominate RMSE.
Tiny pool groups. The pool-quality comparison rests on seven houses.

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text: Final project for STAT 4210 Regression Analysis (Kennesaw State University), December 2024. The report is the main write-up; this page summarizes it.

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text:
Question
Which country-level factors are associated with life expectancy at birth, and how well can a multiple linear regression model predict it?

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text:
The Report


Download the report (PDF) Code and data on GitHub

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text:
Data
The data is World Health Organization (WHO) country-level data for 2021 from the Global Health Observatory and World Health Statistics. Life expectancy at birth is reported for 185 countries, with a mean of 71.3 years (SD 7.1). Japan is highest at 84.46 years and Lesotho lowest at 51.48.



Life expectancy at birth, 2021.


Six predictors were considered:

homicide rate
unintentional poisoning mortality rate
suicide mortality rate
road traffic mortality rate
universal health coverage (UHC) service coverage index
domestic general government health expenditure

Countries missing any variable in a model were dropped (listwise deletion), which left 175 countries for the initial model and 179 for the refined model.

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text:
Approach
Three multiple linear regression models were fit and compared on RMSE, adjusted R², AIC and BIC:

Initial model: all six predictors (175 countries).
Refined model: dropped government health expenditure, which was not significant at the 0.05 level (179 countries).
Final model: the same five predictors, fit with 10-fold cross-validation and with influential outliers removed using a Cook’s distance cutoff of 4/n (171 countries).

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text:
Results






ImportantKey Finding



Five country-level factors explain about 84% of the variation in life expectancy across countries. Universal health coverage is the strongest predictor: each additional point on the UHC service coverage index is associated with about 0.32 more years of life expectancy.


The final model explains about 84% of the variation in life expectancy across countries (adjusted R² = 0.838, residual standard error 2.88 years, F = 177.1 on 5 and 165 degrees of freedom).

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text:
Limitations

Association, not causation. This is observational, cross-sectional data, so the coefficients describe associations between countries and do not show that changing a predictor would change life expectancy.
One year. The 2021 snapshot says nothing about trends over time. Time-series data would be needed to study change.
Narrow set of predictors. Education, income inequality and environmental conditions were not considered.
Missing data. Dropping countries with missing values may bias results if the countries with gaps differ systematically from the rest.
Comparing models. The three models were fit to different numbers of countries, so their AIC and BIC values are not directly comparable. On RMSE and adjusted R² the three models are nearly indistinguishable.

title: Predicting Life Expectancy with Linear Regression
text:
Tools and Data Source
R and Quarto: tidyverse (including ggplot2), caret for cross-validation, car and lmtest for diagnostics, broom, GGally, patchwork, kableExtra, and the maps package for the world map.
Data: World Health Organization, Global Health Observatory and World Health Statistics, used under the CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO licence. This project is not endorsed by or affiliated with WHO.

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
text: On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge posted a computer-checkable proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the most famous open problems in mathematics. I’m checking it myself, from scratch, on my own hardware. This page follows that check live: it updates as each step finishes, and every result on it is quoted from the run’s logs.

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
section: What a Check Can and Can’t Tell You

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
text:
The Five Statements
A proof is only as good as the statement it proves, so the check starts by pinning down exactly what has to be proved. It does that with two separate files.

The challenge is a short file that only states the five theorems. It doesn’t prove anything. Lean won’t accept a theorem without a proof attached, so each one ends in sorry, Lean’s placeholder for a proof left blank.
The solution is the project’s own Main.lean. It states theorems with the same five names and supplies the real proofs.

A checker then compares the two: the statements must mean exactly the same thing, and the proofs must be complete and accepted by the kernel.
Why a separate file? Building the project runs code the project contains, and that code can change what words mean inside it. Kevin Buzzard demonstrates this in talks by redefining exponentiation so that something that looks like Fermat’s Last Theorem becomes trivially “provable”. In the forum thread about this proof, someone showed that one line of notation can make RiemannHypothesis mean True. Reading the project’s own copy of the statements would not catch that. The challenge imports nothing but Mathlib, Lean’s shared math library, whose definition of the Riemann Hypothesis was written long before this project existed. It is built before any project code runs, so nothing in the project can tamper with it.
The five statements, in words:







Theorem
In Words




riemannHypothesis
Mathlib’s RiemannHypothesis: every zero of ζ other than −2, −4, −6, … (and the pole at 1) has real part ½.


riemannZeta_eq_zero_re
The same statement, written out.


LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re
For every modulus N and Dirichlet character χ, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 when Re s > ½, except at the pole χ = 1, s = 1.


LFunction_eq_zero_re
Every zero of every Dirichlet L-function in the strip 0 < Re s < 1 has Re s = ½.


LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive
The same, for primitive characters.









NoteThe challenge file in Lean





import Mathlib

def RiemannZetaZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

def DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

def DirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

def PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := by sorry
theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : RiemannZetaZerosOnLine := by sorry
theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf := by sorry
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : DirichletLZerosOnLine := by sorry
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine := by sorry



I’m not a number theorist, so I don’t rely on my own reading of the last four. They have to match the project’s definitions term for term, which the checkers enforce, and they agree with the version reviewed in public by people who are.
Where this comes from. The challenge-and-solution setup isn’t mine. It is the Lean FRO’s Comparator model, which the community applied to this project in Deicyde/riemann-hypothesis; Kevin Buzzard’s post explains why each part matters. I wrote my challenge file independently, and apart from comments it is identical to the community’s Challenge.lean. It has to be: the statements are fixed by the project, and the checker requires them to match exactly. When I build their file with my Mathlib, it comes out byte for byte the same as theirs.
What this check adds. The challenge file only fixes what is checked. Everything around it is where this run goes further than the basic setup:

Sandboxed build in a fresh VM. The project is compiled with the network off, inside a Landlock sandbox that was tested before use, so the code that builds the proof can’t touch anything else.
Mathlib from source. Mathlib is compiled from source and compared file by file with its official build cache, so the check doesn’t rely on prebuilt files.
Nine checkers. Beyond Comparator’s Lean kernel and nanoda, the proof also goes to con-leche (including its --compare mode, a formally verified second implementation of the statement comparison), con-ron, lean4lean, Pestka and nanoclo.
Secondary checks. An axiom audit that walks every constant itself, a per-module kernel replay, and checks that no source file or tool changed during the run.
Hashes against other runs. My build and export are compared with the hashes other people published, so a match shows we checked the same bytes.

The formal proof itself doesn’t claim more than these five statements. Alpöge’s remark says the method should extend further, but the Lean project proves exactly these five, and those are what get checked.

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
text:
How the Check Works
I treated the project as untrusted code. Building a Lean project runs code it contains (tactics, macros, build commands), so nothing from it ran on my own machine, and nothing that loads it ran outside a sandbox.

A fresh virtual machine with its own kernel. Every tool is pinned to an exact commit and verified, and the project is downloaded and checked inside the VM.
No network once the downloads are done. Mathlib, the math library the project builds on, is then compiled from source and compared file by file with Mathlib’s official build cache.
The statements first. The challenge file is built and exported before any project code runs.
A sandbox for the project. The build runs under Landlock via landrun: it can read its sources and the toolchain and write only its own build folder. I tested that writes elsewhere, reading SSH keys and network connections all fail before starting.
Export, then judge. The compiled proof is exported to a single file. The judges read only that file, so no project code runs while checking. lake comparator checks that the statements match and that only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice are used, then replays the whole proof through Lean’s kernel. Then it goes through every independent checker that fits in the VM’s memory.

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
text:
Findings along the Way






NoteMathlib from Source Matches the Official Cache, with One Exception



Of the 8,700 files in Mathlib’s official build cache, 8,689 are byte-identical to my from-source build. Ten belong to the cache tool itself and aren’t part of the math. One differs: Mathlib/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/Walk/Operations.olean, and only in a single auto-generated lemma, SimpleGraph.Walk.take.eq_2. The other 230 constants in that file match. My build of it is deterministic (rebuilt twice, same bytes), so the cache’s copy was produced differently. Both versions are kernel-checked theorems; this is a reproducibility quirk, not a soundness problem.








NoteA Full Build Needs about 1.7 TB of Bookkeeping



For each module, Lake writes a .setup.json file listing everything it imports. Here that averages about 7 MB, and a sampled estimate over all 175,187 modules is about 1.7 TB. The files compress about 26× with zstd, so this run builds on a compressed btrfs disk.








NoteTwo Problems the Tests Caught



My sandbox wrapper first failed in a way that looked like success: the kernel supports Landlock ABI v6, landrun asked for v10 and refused to start, and every “access denied” test passed because nothing ran at all. A positive control (a command that must succeed) now runs first. Separately, the original checker script counted sorry warnings with the wrong quote characters, so that count could never be non-zero; it’s fixed. The axiom check was never affected.

How I Used AI
It felt right to check an AI-written proof with an AI’s help, and also strange. Claude (Anthropic’s AI) set up and ran this check with me: it wrote the scripts, ran the commands and drafted this page, and I reviewed and directed the work. That is exactly why the check is built so that no single party has to be trusted, including the AI running it. Every result here is read from logs, and the hashes let anyone confirm that the same bytes were checked. It doesn’t settle my mixed feelings about AI, but it does show one thing it can’t take away: a proof that anyone can check for themselves.

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
text:
What Is the Riemann Hypothesis?
Prime numbers (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …) are the building blocks of whole numbers: every whole number is a product of primes in exactly one way. They get rarer as numbers grow, but they never follow a simple pattern. Look at any stretch of numbers and the primes seem scattered almost at random.
In the 1790s, Gauss noticed that the number of primes up to any point follows a smooth curve surprisingly well. In 1859, Bernhard Riemann found a way to describe exactly how far the true count wanders from that curve. The errors are controlled by the zeros of a function now called the Riemann zeta function, written ζ(s). His hypothesis is that all of those zeros (apart from some easy ones at −2, −4, −6, …) sit on a single straight line, where the real part of s is ½. If that’s true, the primes are as evenly spread as they could possibly be. Their irregularity is like the static of a coin-flip sequence, never anything worse.
Why it matters:

It’s the most famous open problem in mathematics. It was on Hilbert’s 1900 list of the century’s key problems, and it is one of the Clay Institute’s seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1 million prize.
A lot of mathematics is built on it. Thousands of published results begin “assuming the Riemann Hypothesis…”. A proof would turn every one of them into a theorem.
It has resisted the best mathematicians for 167 years, despite checks of the first trillions of zeros, which all lie on the line.

(It wouldn’t break internet encryption, a common worry. That depends on how hard it is to factor large numbers, which this doesn’t change.)

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
text:
What Happened
On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge posted a short remark and a 1.4 GB project written in Lean, claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, along with the same statement for every Dirichlet L-function (a whole family of close relatives of ζ). The proof was written with AI, and it is enormous: 175,187 files and about 17 million lines.
No person can read a proof that size. Lean is what makes it checkable anyway. Lean is a proof assistant: a program whose small core, the kernel, accepts a proof only if every single step follows from the rules of logic. That turns “is this proof right?” into a question anyone with a powerful enough computer can answer, as long as they’re careful about exactly what they check.
Within hours, people in the Lean community had built it and run it through several independent checkers (see the forum thread). The most complete public record is Andrew Sutherland’s page, which this page is modelled on.

title: An Independent Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean Proof
text:
Why I’m Checking It Myself
I wanted to do it end to end, for my own understanding, and to feel a small part of history being made.
I also have mixed feelings about it, and a lot of uncertainty about how AI will shape the future. Only weeks ago, in a Numberphile interview, I remember Terence Tao saying he didn’t expect the Riemann Hypothesis to be solved until around 2050. Now there is a claimed proof, written with AI, that Lean’s checkers accept. The only thing anyone can say with certainty is that nothing is off the table.

How the Check Works
I treated the project as untrusted code. Building a Lean project runs code it contains (tactics, macros, build commands), so nothing from it ran on my own machine, and nothing that loads it ran outside a sandbox.

A fresh virtual machine with its own kernel. Every tool is pinned to an exact commit and verified, and the project is downloaded and checked inside the VM.
No network once the downloads are done. Mathlib is then compiled from source and compared file by file with Mathlib’s official build cache.
The statements first. The challenge file is built and exported before any project code runs.
A sandbox for the project. The build runs under Landlock via landrun: it can read its sources and the toolchain and write only its own build folder. Before starting, I tested that writes elsewhere, reading SSH keys and network connections all fail.
Export, then judge. The compiled proof is exported to a single file, and the judges read only that file, so no project code runs while checking. lake comparator checks that the statements match the challenge and that only propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice are used, then replays the whole proof through Lean’s kernel. Then the proof goes through every independent checker that fits in the VM’s memory.



Findings along the Way






NoteMathlib from Source Matches the Official Cache, with One Exception



Of the 8,700 files in Mathlib’s official build cache, 8,689 are byte-identical to my from-source build. Ten belong to the cache tool itself and aren’t part of the math. One differs: Mathlib/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/Walk/Operations.olean, and only in a single auto-generated lemma, SimpleGraph.Walk.take.eq_2. The other 230 constants in that file match. My build of it is deterministic (rebuilt twice, same bytes), so the cache’s copy was produced differently. Both versions are kernel-checked theorems; this is a reproducibility quirk, not a soundness problem.








NoteA Full Build Needs about 1.7 TB of Bookkeeping



For each module, Lake writes a .setup.json file listing everything it imports. Here that averages about 7 MB, and a sampled estimate over all 175,187 modules is about 1.7 TB. The files compress about 26× with zstd, so this run builds on a compressed btrfs disk.








NoteTwo Problems the Tests Caught



My sandbox wrapper first failed in a way that looked like success: the kernel supports Landlock ABI v6, landrun asked for v10 and refused to start, and every “access denied” test passed because nothing ran at all. A positive control (a command that must succeed) now runs first. Separately, the original checker script counted sorry warnings with the wrong quote characters, so that count could never be non-zero; it’s fixed. The axiom check was never affected.
